extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, journalists and legal practitioners interested in UK broadcasting law and censorship cases
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes legal standards from UK Broadcasting Acts and case law governing what may be broadcast (taste/decency, impartiality, party political broadcast rules, and the duties of the broadcast standards body). Useful for evaluating compliance of broadcast material and party political broadcasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nothing included which offends against good taste or decency / likely to encourage or incite crime or disorder / offensive to public feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: From Broadcasting Act 1990 s.6(1)(a): broadcasters must ensure that “nothing is included in its programmes which offends against good taste or decency or is likely to encourage or incite to crime or to lead to disorder or to be offensive to public feeling.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a broad statutory content standard used to justify excluding material judged to offend ordinary standards of taste or to be likely to cause crime/disorder or widespread offence. The Wikipedia article cites the House of Lords description of the ProLife Alliance video as showing “tiny limbs, bloodied and dismembered… certainly disturbing to any person of ordinary sensibilities,” illustrating application of this standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: News must be presented with due accuracy and impartiality
rubrics_metrics.description: From Broadcasting Act 1990 s.6(1)(b): “that any news given (in whatever form) in its programmes is presented with due accuracy and impartiality.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory requirement for factual reporting: accuracy and impartiality are explicit legal expectations for news content carried by licensed services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due impartiality preserved in matters of political/industrial controversy or current public policy
rubrics_metrics.description: From Broadcasting Act 1990 s.6(1)(c): broadcasters must preserve “due impartiality … as respects matters of political or industrial controversy or relating to current public policy.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Places an onus on licensees to avoid partisan presentation in programming touching on political controversy or public policy; relevant to both editorial programming and rules governing party political broadcasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licence conditions to include party political broadcasts and observe Commission rules
rubrics_metrics.description: From Broadcasting Act 1990: regional Channel 3 and Channel 4/5 licences shall include conditions requiring the licence holder to include party political broadcasts and to observe such rules with respect to party political broadcasts as the Commission may determine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory framework authorises the regulator to set detailed rules (e.g., who may broadcast, length and frequency) and mandates broadcasters to carry allocated party political broadcasts under licence conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commission may determine which parties may broadcast and the length/frequency of broadcasts
rubrics_metrics.description: From Broadcasting Act 1990 s.6(3): subject to other provisions the Commission may determine “the political parties on whose behalf party political broadcasts may be made” and “in relation to any political party … the length and frequency of such broadcasts.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grants the regulator discretion to allocate broadcast access and to set quantitative rules for party political broadcasts; relevant when disputes arise over entitlement or allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSC duty to monitor portrayal of violence and sexual conduct and standards of taste and decency
rubrics_metrics.description: From Broadcasting Act 1996 s.109(1): the Broadcasting Standards Commission (BSC) “shall do… with a view to enabling the BSC to make reports on the portrayal of violence and sexual conduct in, and the standards of taste and decency attained by, such programmes generally.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandates proactive monitoring and reporting by the standards body on how violence/sexual conduct are portrayed and on overall taste/decency standards in applicable programmes.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSC duty to consider complaints about unjust or unfair treatment and unwarranted infringement of privacy
rubrics_metrics.description: From Broadcasting Act 1996 s.110(1): the BSC must consider complaints made in accordance with the Act that relate to “unjust or unfair treatment in programmes … or to unwarranted infringement of privacy in, or in connection with the obtaining of material included in, such programmes.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes specific complaint categories the standards body must adjudicate: unfair/unjust treatment and privacy infringements tied to programme material or how it was obtained.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSC duty to consider complaints about failures to attain standards of taste and decency
rubrics_metrics.description: From Broadcasting Act 1996 s.110(2)(b): the BSC must consider complaints relating to “alleged failures on the part of such programmes to attain standards of taste and decency.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides an explicit enforcement route for viewers to complain when programmes are alleged not to meet statutory taste and decency standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material that is disturbing to persons of ordinary sensibilities may be excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: As described in the House of Lords’ characterization of the submitted ProLife Alliance video: graphic depictions (e.g., “tiny limbs, bloodied and dismembered… plain[ly] recognisable”) were considered “certainly disturbing to any person of ordinary sensibilities.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative application: graphic medical/abortion imagery can be judged as disturbing to ordinary viewers and therefore fall foul of taste/decency standards; courts may describe content in terms of ordinary sensibilities when assessing compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcasters may decline to show material that could be offensive or disturbing to a large number of viewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical broadcaster rationale in the case: the broadcasters declined to show the video on the grounds that it could have been offensive or disturbing to a large number of viewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational criterion used by broadcasters when exercising editorial judgment under statutory duties — weighing likely public offence/disturbance across audience against freedom of expression and political-broadcast obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness in allocation of election/party political broadcasts (broadcasters should not unfairly deny allocated broadcasts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Court of Appeal ruling in favour of ProLife Alliance stated the BBC had acted unfairly in denying them one election broadcast in Wales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal standard concerning fair treatment in the allocation and delivery of party political broadcasts; denial of an allocated broadcast may give rise to successful judicial review where unfairness is shown.
